events.title: Bush carries Ohio
events.text: George W. Bush carried Ohio by three and a half points on his way to the presidency.

events.title: Ohio decides 2004
events.text: Bush won Ohio by about two points, and with it a second term.

events.title: Strickland elected
events.text: Ted Strickland won the governorship with 60.5 percent; he is the last Democrat elected governor of Ohio.

events.title: Brown unseats DeWine
events.text: Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, defeated Senator Mike DeWine for a U.S. Senate seat.

events.title: Obama carries Ohio
events.text: Barack Obama carried Ohio by 4.6 points; Hamilton County voted Democratic for the first time since 1964.

events.title: Kasich elected
events.text: John Kasich, a Republican, defeated Governor Strickland.

events.title: Obama again
events.text: Obama carried Ohio by three points, as he won a second term.

events.title: Trump by eight
events.text: Donald Trump carried Ohio by 8.1 points; Trumbull County, long Democratic, voted for him.

events.title: DeWine elected
events.text: Mike DeWine beat Richard Cordray for governor, 50.4 to 46.7 percent.

events.title: Split ticket
events.text: The same day, Sherrod Brown won a third Senate term with 53.4 percent.

events.title: A health director
events.text: Governor DeWine named Amy Acton director of the Ohio Department of Health, the first woman in the post.

events.title: Polls closed
events.text: On the eve of the 17 March primary, Acton ordered polling places closed; in-person voting was postponed.

events.title: Stay at home
events.text: On 22 March Acton signed a statewide stay-at-home order.

events.title: Acton resigns
events.text: On 11 June Acton stepped down as health director and became the governor's health adviser.

events.title: Mahoning turns
events.text: Mahoning County, home to Youngstown, voted Republican for president for the first time since 1972.

events.title: The streak ends
events.text: Ohio voted for Donald Trump as Joe Biden won the presidency, ending a run of correct picks that began in 1964.

events.title: Intel's chip plant
events.text: Intel announced a chip factory at New Albany; in 2025 it pushed its opening back to 2030–31.

events.title: DeWine re-elected
events.text: DeWine beat Nan Whaley, the former mayor of Dayton, with 62.4 percent.

events.title: Issue 1 rejected
events.text: In August voters rejected a 60 percent threshold for constitutional amendments, 57 to 43.

events.title: Abortion amendment
events.text: In November voters wrote abortion rights into the state constitution, 56.8 to 43.2 percent.

events.title: Marijuana legalised
events.text: The same day, Issue 2 legalised recreational marijuana with 57.2 percent.

events.title: Moreno beats Brown
events.text: Bernie Moreno defeated Senator Sherrod Brown, 50.1 to 46.5 percent.

events.title: Redistricting rejected
events.text: Voters turned down an independent redistricting commission, 53.7 to 46.3 percent.

events.title: Trump by eleven
events.text: Trump carried Ohio by 11.2 points; Trumbull gave him a margin of nearly seventeen.

events.title: Acton files
events.text: On 7 January Amy Acton filed to run for governor as a Democrat.

events.title: Ramaswamy leaves DOGE
events.text: On Inauguration Day, 20 January, Vivek Ramaswamy left the Department of Government Efficiency.

events.title: Ramaswamy launches
events.text: On 24 February Ramaswamy launched his campaign in West Chester Township; President Trump endorsed him that day.

events.title: Party endorsement
events.text: On 9 May the Ohio Republican Party's central committee endorsed Ramaswamy, 60 votes to 3.

events.title: Yost withdraws
events.text: On 16 May Attorney General Dave Yost ended his campaign for governor.

events.title: A flat income tax
events.text: On 30 June DeWine signed a budget that set a flat 2.75 percent income tax from 2026.

events.title: Tressel stays out
events.text: On 19 September Lieutenant Governor Jim Tressel said he would not run for governor.

events.title: Veto overridden
events.text: On 1 October the Senate completed an override of DeWine's veto on property-tax levies.

events.title: Ryan stays out
events.text: On 21 November former congressman Tim Ryan said he would not run, leaving Acton unopposed.

events.title: Property-tax bills
events.text: On 19 December DeWine signed five bills to limit property-tax increases.

events.title: McColley chosen
events.text: On 6 January Ramaswamy chose Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, of Napoleon, as his running mate.

events.title: Pepper chosen
events.text: On 7 January Acton chose David Pepper, a former Ohio Democratic Party chair from Cincinnati, as hers.

events.title: DeWine endorses
events.text: On 7 January Governor DeWine endorsed Ramaswamy.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 5 May Ramaswamy won the Republican primary with 82 percent; Acton was unopposed; Don Kissick won the Libertarian primary.

events.title: No debate
events.text: On 2 September Ramaswamy accepted invitations to debate from CNN and WLWT; Acton declined.

events.title: Canfield Fair
events.text: On 6 September a man carrying two handguns pushed through the crowd at Acton's event; he was charged with assault, and both campaigns condemned violence.

events.title: Gas-tax holiday
events.text: Both nominees backed a 90-day suspension of the state gas tax, signed on 1 October.

events.title: Trump in Vandalia
events.text: On 3 October President Trump rallied with Ramaswamy and Senator Jon Husted in Vandalia.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: Early in-person voting began on 6 October; by 20 October more than 676,000 Ohioans had voted early in person or by mail.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Ohioans choose between Ramaswamy, Acton, Kissick and four write-in candidates.

eras: Kasich, Trump and a turning state
A pandemic, ballot fights and an open seat
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results). It is a simplification: Ohio elects its governor in its own race, in a midterm year, and its voters have often split their tickets (in 2018 they re-elected a Democratic senator and chose a Republican governor on the same day), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Ohio, so outer states are cut at the edge.
